status: drafted by a single agent grounded in the real extracted Geneva 1560 verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Geneva/3_john_76.json); not yet adversarially fact-checked or user-confirmed
notes: This Geneva 1560 rendering of 3 John is content-identical to the KJV's version already indexed in this project (same one chapter, same 14 verses, same four named figures, same events, no deuterocanonical or structural differences of the kind found elsewhere in this translation project) — only the archaic 1560 English orthography differs (e.g. "trueth" for truth, "vnto" for unto, "yncke and pen" for ink and pen, "reioyced" for rejoiced, "beseemeth" for beseemeth/becometh). Because of that, this book keeps the same four person-type manager tiers as the KJV index (the Elder, Gaius, Diotrephes, Demetrius) plus one collective submanager (the unnamed traveling brethren/strangers Gaius supported) — no law/theme tiers, since the letter is personal exhortation and church-politics narrative in miniature, not doctrine or ritual instruction. All character ids are suffixed "_geneva_3john" to avoid colliding with the existing KJV CharacterIndex ids for the same names. Naming-collision flags carried over and re-verified against this translation's own text: this Gaius is never identified in the Geneva text with the Gaius of Corinth, Macedonia, or Derbe found elsewhere in the NT; this Demetrius is never identified with the silversmith of Acts 19; "the Elder" is only ever self-designated that way here (matching 2 John 1:1 in this same translation) — traditional identification with John the Apostle is not asserted as textual fact. No genealogy (father/mother/spouses/children) is stated anywhere in this book for any figure in this translation either, so every genealogy field is null/empty, and ageEvents are empty across the board for the same reason — it is a short personal letter, not a narrative with biographical detail.

characters.name: The Elder

verses.note: "The Elder vnto the beloued Gaius, whom I loue in the trueth" — opens the letter addressing Gaius directly.
Wishes chiefly that Gaius "prosperedst and faredst well as thy soule prospereth."
"Reioyced greatly" when brethren testified Gaius walks in the truth; says he has no greater joy than hearing his "sonnes walke in veritie."
States such traveling brethren "ought to receiue," that we might be "helpers to the trueth"; says he wrote to the Church but Diotrephes, who loves preeminence, "receiueth vs not."

Says if he comes he will recall Diotrephes' deeds: "pratling against vs with malicious wordes," refusing to receive the brethren himself, forbidding others who would, and thrusting them out of the Church.
Bears record himself of Demetrius' good report, "and ye know that our record is true."
Has many things to write but "will not with yncke and pen write vnto thee"; trusts he shall shortly see Gaius and "speake mouth to mouth"; sends peace and greetings, "greete the friends by name."

funFacts: Uses the archaic Geneva-1560 spelling "yncke and pen" (3 John 1:13) for the same phrase later modernized to "ink and pen" in the KJV — the physical act of letter-writing he is choosing to forgo in favor of a face-to-face visit.

characters.name: Gaius

verses.note: Addressed as "the beloued Gaius, whom I loue in the trueth."
The Elder wishes he "faredst well as thy soule prospereth."
Brethren testified he "walkest in the trueth"; called one of the Elder's spiritual "sonnes."
Commended: "thou doest faithfully, whatsoeuer thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers," whose testimony of his love reached the Churches.
Urged, if he brings the travelers on their journey, to do it "as it beseemeth according to God," and he "shalt doe well."
Exhorted: "follow not that which is euill, but that which is good: he that doeth well, is of God: but he that doeth euill, hath not seene God" — set against Diotrephes' example.

funFacts: Distinct in this translation, as in the KJV, from the other New Testament men named Gaius (Corinth, Macedonia, Derbe) — the Geneva text never links this Gaius to any of them.

characters.name: Diotrephes

verses.note: Described as one "which loueth to haue the preeminence among them," and who "receiueth vs not" — rejects the Elder's authority.

If the Elder comes he will recall Diotrephes' deeds: "pratling against vs with malicious wordes," not content with that, refusing the brethren himself, forbidding others who would receive them, and "thrusteth them out of the Church."

funFacts: The Geneva text gives no genealogy, prior history, or stated outcome for him beyond this one letter — his entire textual presence is this single confrontation over hospitality and standing in the Church.

characters.name: Demetrius

verses.note: "Demetrius hath good report of al men, and of the trueth it selfe: yea, and wee our selues beare recorde, and ye know that our record is true."

funFacts: Distinct in this translation, as in the KJV, from Demetrius the silversmith of Ephesus (Acts 19) — the Geneva text draws no connection between the two men.

characters.name: The Brethren and Strangers

verses.note: Received hospitality from Gaius as "the brethren, and to strangers," and "bare witnesse of thy loue before the Churches."
"Because that for his Names sake they went forth, and tooke nothing of the Gentiles."
The Elder states such travelers "ought to receiue," that we might be "helpers to the trueth."

funFacts: A collective group of traveling missionaries, never individually named or differentiated in the Geneva text — kept as one entry rather than invented individuals, per the established methodology.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

friends_greeting.note: "The friends salute thee. Greete the friends by name" — unnamed collective well-wishers on both ends of the correspondence, not individually identified in the Geneva text.

spiritual_sonnes.note: "My sonnes" — the Elder's spiritual converts/disciples in general (Geneva's rendering of the KJV's "my children"), not named individuals; no biological family is mentioned for the Elder anywhere in this letter.

the_church.note: "The Church" the Elder wrote to, and from which Diotrephes casts out willing brethren — the congregation/institution itself, not a person, so kept out of the character list.
